titleStmt.title: ANI-1: an extensible neural network potential with DFT accuracy at force field computational cost

Olexandr Isayev

bibl.title: ANI-1: an extensible neural network potential with DFT accuracy at force field computational cost

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: transferable atomistic potentials for organic molecules - whether a network trained on quantum-mechanical energies for small molecules can predict energies for larger ones it never saw
span.quote: Through a series of case studies, we show that ANI-1 is chemically accurate compared to reference DFT calculations on much larger molecular systems (up to 54 atoms) than those included in the training data set.

span.label: whether the accuracy-for-speed trade that empirical potentials have always made can be avoided, rather than merely moved
span.quote: One of the grand challenges in modern theoretical chemistry is designing and implementing approximations that expedite ab initio methods without loss of accuracy.

span.label: the ANI method - atomic environment vectors from modified Behler-Parrinello symmetry functions, plus Normal Mode Sampling - and ANI-1, a potential trained on 17.2 million DFT conformations of molecules up to 8 heavy atoms
span.quote: Through a series of case studies, we show that ANI-1 is chemically accurate compared to reference DFT calculations on much larger molecular systems (up to 54 atoms) than those included in the training data set.

span.label: method
span.quote: Through a series of case studies, we show that ANI-1 is chemically accurate compared to reference DFT calculations on much larger molecular systems (up to 54 atoms) than those included in the training data set.

span.label: transferability - a fitted potential's ability to hold outside the domain it was fitted in, which this field has no systematic way to estimate
span.quote: Furthermore, each application of FF and EP needs to be carefully pondered, as their accuracy varies among different systems. In fact, performing benchmarks to determine the optimal FF combination for the problem at hand is usually unavoidable. Unfortunately, there are no systematic ways for improving or estimating the transferability of EPs.

span.label: train atom-type-specific networks on atomic environment vectors, sample conformations by randomly perturbing along normal modes, and test only on molecules larger than any in the training set
span.term: train atom-type-specific networks on atomic environment vectors, sample conformations by randomly perturbing along normal modes, and test only on molecules larger than any in the training set
span.quote: In practice, NMS works best when generating windows of the potential surface of many molecules to be used in the training of the same ANI potential. The reasoning behind this is as follows: if any interactions are missed or not sampled well by NMS, it is possible that other molecules in the data set contain the same or similar interactions. Therefore, the accuracy of using such a sampling method is dependent on not only the number of points per window but also the number of distinct molecules included in the data set.

span.label: a sorted coulomb matrix sized for the largest training molecule leaves elements that are constant zero throughout training; a larger test molecule makes those elements non-zero, feeding values into network parameters that were never updated, so the output is arbitrary rather than merely inaccurate
span.term: untrained parameters reached only by larger inputs
span.quote: For baseline 1, this is caused by the coulomb matrix having elements which remain a constant zero throughout training, yet when a larger molecule is tested on it, those elements have non-zero values. These non-zero values are then fed into untrained network parameters, which yields arbitrary results.

span.label: symmetry functions that sum over all neighbours identically leave the network unable to tell a carbon from a hydrogen at a given distance, so the same vector element means different things in different molecules and training cannot resolve it
span.quote: For baseline 2, the problem comes from the fact that the AEVs have an inability to differentiate between atom types, creating confusion during the learning process.

span.label: MD follows one well-defined path across the potential surface, so a data set built from it is a sample of that path rather than of the surface; overcoming the bias requires a trajectory long enough to lose its own starting point
span.quote: Because of this, utilizing MD would follow a well-defined trajectory along the potential surface and would lead to sampling biased to the specific trajectory. Thus, a very long trajectory is required to overcome this bias.

span.label: normal mode sampling can miss interactions in any single molecule, but a data set of many molecules contains the same interaction in other contexts - so accuracy depends on the number of distinct molecules and not only on points per molecule
span.term: cross-molecule overlap covering a sampler's gaps
span.quote: In practice, NMS works best when generating windows of the potential surface of many molecules to be used in the training of the same ANI potential. The reasoning behind this is as follows: if any interactions are missed or not sampled well by NMS, it is possible that other molecules in the data set contain the same or similar interactions. Therefore, the accuracy of using such a sampling method is dependent on not only the number of points per window but also the number of distinct molecules included in the data set.

span.label: the headline 0.6 kcal/mol holds only within 30 kcal/mol of each molecule's energy minimum; across the whole sampled range the RMSE is 1.8
span.quote: Fig. 4A is a correlation plot of the computed ANI-1 energies, E cmp, vs. the DFT reference energies, E ref. The ANI-1 potential achieves an RMSE of only 1.8 kcal mol–1 over the entire random sampling. Fig. 4B–D provides the same comparison but for popular semi-empirical methods to the DFT reference energies. If only relative energies within 30.0 kcal mol–1 of the minimum energy are considered, the ANI-1, DFTB, PM6, and AM1 methods obtain an RMSE of 0.6, 2.4, 3.6, and 4.2 kcal mol–1, respectively.

span.label: the potential covers only H, C, N and O, and only near-equilibrium conformations, because full sampling of each structure's potential surface is near intractable
span.quote: Therefore, we limit the scope of this study to a specific class of systems, namely organic molecules with four atom types: H, C, N, and O. We also restrict our data set to near equilibrium conformations, since a full sampling of each structure's potential surface increases the number of data points required for training to a near intractable level.

span.label: Normal Mode Sampling is stated by the authors to be simply an approximation for generating structures, not a sampling of the true potential surface
span.quote: The choice of temperature is dependent on the intended use of the ANI potential being trained. However, it should be noted that this method of sampling the potential surface of a molecule is simply an approximation for generating structures.

span.label: its accuracy is a property of the training data rather than of the method - the authors say so, and make the improvement path more data rather than a better model
span.quote: The accuracy of the ANI method is heavily dependent on the data used during training. Thus, continuing to augment the ANI-1 data set with new molecules and including more atomic numbers will improve the accuracy of the trained ANI potential further as well as extend the method to new chemical environments.

span.label: the error had not plateaued at the largest data set built, so the reported accuracy is a point on a curve still moving rather than a converged property
span.quote: More important than the low errors to the training, validation, and test sets, it shows that the extensibility of ANI potentials increase with data set size, and does not plateau up to the current data set size.

span.label: deep learning architectures and their training machinery - mini-batches, ADAM, max-norm regularisation, early stopping - carried from image and speech recognition into quantum chemistry
span.quote: This cost function was chosen because of its robustness in handling outliers in data sets, a property that achieves 2 to 4 times lower error upon training an ANI potential.

span.label: normal mode analysis, carried from vibrational spectroscopy into a sampler for generating training conformations
span.quote: The choice of temperature is dependent on the intended use of the ANI potential being trained. However, it should be noted that this method of sampling the potential surface of a molecule is simply an approximation for generating structures.

span.label: testing only on molecules LARGER than any in the training set - every case study uses more than eight heavy atoms, where training stopped at eight
span.note: eliminates: an accuracy that holds only inside the size range the network was trained on · outcome: held
span.quote: Through a series of case studies, we show that ANI-1 is chemically accurate compared to reference DFT calculations on much larger molecular systems (up to 54 atoms) than those included in the training data set.

span.label: two baselines carried through the same training - a coulomb-matrix MLP, and an ANI network with atom types NOT differentiated - so the contribution of each design choice is separable
span.note: eliminates: the whole architecture being credited with a gain that the representation or one design choice supplies · outcome: held
span.quote: ANI-1, when trained on the full ANI-1 training set, achieves a total energy RMSE of 1.9 kcal mol–1 while baseline 1 and baseline 2 achieve a RMSE of 493.7 kcal mol–1 and 6.6 kcal mol–1, respectively. While the baselines perform better on the ANI-1 test set, as seen in ESI Fig. S4,† their performance on the GDB-10 test set shows that both suffer from an inability to extend their learned interactions to larger molecules.

span.label: comparison against three incumbent semi-empirical methods, DFTB, PM6 and AM1, on every case study rather than against DFT alone
span.note: eliminates: a neural potential compared only against the reference it was trained to imitate, and never against the methods it is meant to replace · outcome: held
span.quote: As expected both semi-empirical methods severely underestimate dihedral rotation barriers, and in the case of lisdexamfetamine give an unrealistic shape of potential surface.

span.label: checking that the potential surface is SMOOTH and not merely low-error, because a potential with the right energies and the wrong curvature is useless for dynamics
span.note: eliminates: a potential with the right energies and the wrong curvature passing as usable for molecular dynamics · outcome: held
span.quote: However, to be useful in molecular dynamics simulations, the ANI-1 potential must not only have a low error, but must also produce a very smooth physically meaningful surface.

span.label: training-set size varied to check whether accuracy had converged, rather than reporting the largest run alone
span.note: eliminates: an accuracy figure reported from the largest training run without showing whether it had converged · outcome: partial
span.quote: More important than the low errors to the training, validation, and test sets, it shows that the extensibility of ANI potentials increase with data set size, and does not plateau up to the current data set size.

span.label: transferability
span.quote: Furthermore, each application of FF and EP needs to be carefully pondered, as their accuracy varies among different systems. In fact, performing benchmarks to determine the optimal FF combination for the problem at hand is usually unavoidable. Unfortunately, there are no systematic ways for improving or estimating the transferability of EPs.

span.label: ANI-1
span.quote: Through a series of case studies, we show that ANI-1 is chemically accurate compared to reference DFT calculations on much larger molecular systems (up to 54 atoms) than those included in the training data set.

span.label: baseline 1
span.quote: ANI-1, when trained on the full ANI-1 training set, achieves a total energy RMSE of 1.9 kcal mol–1 while baseline 1 and baseline 2 achieve a RMSE of 493.7 kcal mol–1 and 6.6 kcal mol–1, respectively. While the baselines perform better on the ANI-1 test set, as seen in ESI Fig. S4,† their performance on the GDB-10 test set shows that both suffer from an inability to extend their learned interactions to larger molecules.

span.label: NMS
span.quote: In practice, NMS works best when generating windows of the potential surface of many molecules to be used in the training of the same ANI potential. The reasoning behind this is as follows: if any interactions are missed or not sampled well by NMS, it is possible that other molecules in the data set contain the same or similar interactions. Therefore, the accuracy of using such a sampling method is dependent on not only the number of points per window but also the number of distinct molecules included in the data set.

span.label: ReaxFF
span.quote: One exception to this is the ReaxFF force field, which is capable of studying chemical reactions and transition states. However, ReaxFF, like most reactive force fields, must generally be reparameterized from system to system and therefore lacks an “out-of-the-box” level of transferability.

span.label: SFs
span.quote: We suggest two reasons for the lack of transferability of the SFs. Firstly, as originally defined, SFs lack the functional form to create recognizable features (spatial arrangements of atoms found in common organic molecules, e.g. a benzene ring, alkenes, functional groups) in the molecular representation, a problem that can prevent a neural network from learning interactions in one molecule and then transferring its knowledge to another molecule upon prediction. Secondly, the SFs have limited atomic number differentiation, which empirically hinders training in complex chemical environments.

span.label: DTNN
span.quote: So far, the DTNN model was only trained to small test data sets to show the model could predict molecular energies in specific cases, i.e. equilibrium geometries of organic molecules or the energy along the path of short QM molecular dynamics trajectories. In our experience, training to trajectories can bias the fitness of a model to the specific trajectory used for training, especially along short trajectories. Also, DTNN potentials were not shown to predict energies for larger systems than those included in the training set.

span.label: coulomb matrices
span.quote: Also, the typical inputs, such as internal coordinates or coulomb matrices, lack transferability to different molecules since the input size to a neural network must remain constant.

span.label: overtraining
span.quote: The choice of network architecture also plays a major role in how well a potential performs. Too small of a network reduces the flexibility of the function which can hinder performance and too large can lead to bad generalization across structures due to overtraining, especially on small data sets. With larger data sets, a bigger and more flexible network can be used to yield better results.

span.label: network architecture
span.quote: The choice of network architecture also plays a major role in how well a potential performs. Too small of a network reduces the flexibility of the function which can hinder performance and too large can lead to bad generalization across structures due to overtraining, especially on small data sets. With larger data sets, a bigger and more flexible network can be used to yield better results.

span.label: cost function
span.quote: This cost function was chosen because of its robustness in handling outliers in data sets, a property that achieves 2 to 4 times lower error upon training an ANI potential.

span.label: semi-empirical methods
span.quote: As expected both semi-empirical methods severely underestimate dihedral rotation barriers, and in the case of lisdexamfetamine give an unrealistic shape of potential surface.

span.label: RMSE of ANI-1 against DFT - OVER THE WHOLE SAMPLING: 1.8 kcal/mol across 8,245 conformations of 134 ten-heavy-atom molecules
span.quote: Fig. 4A is a correlation plot of the computed ANI-1 energies, E cmp, vs. the DFT reference energies, E ref. The ANI-1 potential achieves an RMSE of only 1.8 kcal mol–1 over the entire random sampling. Fig. 4B–D provides the same comparison but for popular semi-empirical methods to the DFT reference energies. If only relative energies within 30.0 kcal mol–1 of the minimum energy are considered, the ANI-1, DFTB, PM6, and AM1 methods obtain an RMSE of 0.6, 2.4, 3.6, and 4.2 kcal mol–1, respectively.

span.label: RMSE of ANI-1 against DFT - WITHIN 30 kcal/mol OF THE MINIMUM: 0.6 kcal/mol. The number the conclusion quotes, and the window is stated with it
span.quote: Fig. 4A is a correlation plot of the computed ANI-1 energies, E cmp, vs. the DFT reference energies, E ref. span.label: "the better model" - ON THE ANI-1 TEST SET: the two baselines perform better than ANI-1
span.quote: ANI-1, when trained on the full ANI-1 training set, achieves a total energy RMSE of 1.9 kcal mol–1 while baseline 1 and baseline 2 achieve a RMSE of 493.7 kcal mol–1 and 6.6 kcal mol–1, respectively. While the baselines perform better on the ANI-1 test set, as seen in ESI Fig. S4,† their performance on the GDB-10 test set shows that both suffer from an inability to extend their learned interactions to larger molecules.
